title: How a fintech product should write an about page
metaTitle: How to write a fintech product about page
excerpt: A fintech about page should name the people accountable for the money product and say why that matters. Skip the origin story unless it changes the decision to start.
alt: Curved library shelves packed with books, seen from a balcony, a record of who did the work for a page that has to name the people behind a product.
caption: Library shelves from a balcony. An about page should be a record, not a myth. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What is the job of a fintech about page?
faqs.answer: The job is to show that specific people stand behind the product a buyer may trust with money. Name who does the work and why this buyer should care. The page is proof of accountability. It is not a place to retell the company's personality.

faqs.question: Should we include our founding story?
faqs.answer: Include it only when a fact in the story changes the decision to open an account or talk to sales. A relevant fact might be that the founders ran the operation this product replaces, or that a named person is responsible for exceptions. A garage anecdote that does not change the decision can wait.

faqs.question: Do we need photos of the team?
faqs.answer: Use photographs of the real people in the roles you are asking a buyer to trust. A portrait with a name and a responsibility is useful. A collage of unnamed smiles, or stock photography of a handshake, makes the page look like it is hiding the team. If someone should not be public, do not invent a substitute face.

markdown:
A fintech product about page is proof that people stand behind the offer. Name who does the work, and say why a buyer who may trust you with money should care. Then give them a way to start an account or talk to sales.

Skip the origin myth unless a fact in it changes that decision. A story about a late night and a whiteboard does not answer who is responsible when a payout fails.

## Who is accountable

Open with the people, not the adjective. A buyer wants to know who operates the product, who reviews an exception, and who the company is in the legal sense. Those can be three short lines. They should be true on the day you publish them.

Google's helpful-content guidance puts trust at the center of what it calls experience, expertise, authoritativeness, and trustworthiness, and it gives extra weight when a topic can affect someone's financial stability. The same page asks a practical "who" question: is it obvious who created this, and can a reader learn more about those people? An about page is the natural place to answer. A fintech site that hides the answer in a footer link called "company" has treated accountability as decoration.

Use names where you can. A named head of support, a named compliance lead, a named founder who still reads exception queues. Roles are enough when a name would be unsafe or misleading, but the role must be specific. "Leadership team" is not a role. "The person who approves a new payout corridor" is.

If a partner bank, a sponsor, or a licensed entity does part of the work, say so in the same breath as your own team. Buyers are not offended by a clear split. They are offended by discovering the split inside an application. Write the split the way you would explain it to a finance lead in the first meeting.

## Why this buyer should care

The second job of the page is relevance. A team biography that could be pasted onto a design studio or a food brand has not said why a money buyer is here. Connect each person to a responsibility this buyer feels.

"Ava ran payout operations at a marketplace before building this" tells a marketplace founder why Ava's judgment matters. "Ava loves coffee and long runs" tells them nothing they can use. Human detail is welcome after the responsibility is clear. It is a poor substitute for it.

Write to one buyer, the one the rest of the site is for. If your product serves marketplaces, the about page should sound like you have sat with a marketplace operator. Mention the failure they fear. A file that does not reconcile. A seller who cannot see why a payout is late. A bank partner who asks questions your team cannot answer. Then show which person on your side owns that fear. Care, on this page, is ownership.

Keep the company description to a few sentences. What you do, who it is for, and what you refuse. The refusal belongs here as well as on the services page, because a buyer often opens the about page to see whether the refusal is real. A team that will not take certain risk, certain countries, or certain "move fast" requests should say so before the sales call.

## When an origin story earns its place

An origin story earns its place when it contains a decision the buyer can inspect. You built this because you were the operator who stayed up reconciling payouts, and the product still refuses to hide a failed transfer. That story changes the read of the product. You built this because the financial system is broken and you are passionate about change. That story changes nothing a buyer can check.

If you tell it, tell it short. One scene. One constraint. One thing that is still true in the product. Put it after the accountability lines, not before. A reader who leaves in the first moments should still have seen a name. A 600-word myth above the fold asks for time you have not earned.

Do not invent a customer in the origin story. Do not invent a regulatory close call. If the true story is ordinary, an ordinary page is the honest page. "We are a small team that operates payouts for marketplaces, and here is who answers" can be the whole story. Ordinary and specific beats cinematic and vague.

## Credentials without a trophy wall

Credentials help when they map to the job. A license number, a years-in-role fact, a former operator's domain. They do not help as a collage of university logos and conference badges. A buyer under financial stress, or simply careful with company money, is looking for relevance. A badge does not explain who reviews a hold.

If you list press or investors, add the fact that matters. "Backed by X" is gossip unless you say what that changes for the buyer. It usually changes nothing about a payout. Prefer a sentence about capital, runway, or a partner only when your counsel agrees it is accurate and useful. Leave the rest off. An about page is not a pitch deck that leaked.

Awards and headcount are the same trap. A number you cannot explain is a number to omit. "Twelve people, six of whom have run payout operations" is a fact with a point. "A world-class team" is a mood. Choose the fact.

Photography should match the claim. Real rooms, real faces, current. Thomas Bewick, a public Hanabi project, is a heritage subject carried onto a modern editorial site. The transferable lesson is narrow and useful: show the actual people and the actual material, not a costume of seriousness. A fintech about page in rented suits, shot like a bank advertisement from another decade, tells the buyer you do not have a picture of the work.

## The company and the product in one frame

The about page should meet the product, not replace it. Somewhere on the page, show the same product state the homepage shows, and say which of these people are responsible for it. A team page that never mentions the ledger, the card, or the payout is a social page. The buyer came to decide about money.

Link to the security note, the partner bank, and the status of funds in words you have already used elsewhere. Do not introduce a new metaphor here. If the homepage says you do not hold funds, the about page should not say you "look after customer money" in a warmer voice. Warmth that contradicts the fact is how trust breaks.

Give the page one action. Start an account if the reader is ready, or talk to sales if the next step is a conversation. The action can sit after the names. "Talk to Priya about a payout exception" is better than a generic contact button if Priya is the person you just described and that is the true path. Do not offer five humans as five doors unless each door is a real responsibility. A buyer should not have to guess which name receives the money question.

## What the page should refuse to be

Refuse the culture page as a substitute. Values lists are fine when each value has a behavior. "We review every failed payout the same day" is a value a buyer can test. "We put customers first" is a poster. If you want values, write three behaviors and stop.

Refuse the timeline that exists to look inevitable. Founded, first customer, fundraise, new office. None of that tells a new buyer who answers on a Tuesday. A short timeline is allowed when the dates are regulatory or operational facts: when you received a license, when you started settling in a corridor, when a partner changed. Mark those. Skip the rest.

Refuse humor that makes light of loss, freezes, or "the banks." The buyer may be annoyed at banks too. They still want a straight page. A joke in the hero is a signal that the team is performing ease it has not earned from this reader.

Hanabi writes and builds pages like this as part of a brand and site engagement, not as a biography exercise. If you want help deciding which names and which facts belong above the fold, book [an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min). Bring the current about page and the sentence you use when a customer asks who is responsible.

## Keep the page maintainable

An about page rots when people leave and the portraits stay. Put a review on the same cadence as access reviews. When a role changes, change the page the same week. A stale named owner is worse than a role with no portrait, because it tells a careful buyer the site is not operated.

Store the portraits, the bios, and the legal description somewhere the team can find them after launch. On a Hanabi project, that place is the client portal: brand files, docs, and updates, not a folder in a chat. The public page should be easy to correct. A hardcoded collage that needs a developer for every title change will go stale, and a stale about page is a trust problem, not a content problem.

Write the page so a new teammate can edit a bio without redesigning the grid. One type style. One image crop. One length. Constraint is what keeps the page honest six months later, when the original writer is busy and someone still has to add the new support lead before a buyer notices the gap.

Once the people are clear, the buyer will look for evidence that the product has survived a real constraint. [Proof pages for a fintech product](/blog/proof-pages-for-a-fintech-product) is the next piece: how to show the decision, not a screenshot with no story.
